\section[ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum]{ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum — clever, talented}

\label{lesson:LA-C406-ingeniosus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to say repeatedly, then the Latin for a task.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum}
\textbf{ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum} — \textquotedblleft{}clever, talented\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Puer ingeniōsus omnia celeriter discit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The clever boy learns everything quickly.}
\end{quote}

\emph{ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum}, built on \emph{ingenium}, natural talent. English \emph{ingenious}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ingeniōsus} is built on \emph{ingenium} \textquotedblleft{}inborn talent\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), with the ending \emph{-ōsus} \textquotedblleft{}full of\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{ingenious} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to say repeatedly, then the Latin for a task, then say \emph{ingeniōsus, ingeniōsa, ingeniōsum} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[attentus, attenta, attentum]{attentus, attenta, attentum — attentive, intent; careful with money}

\label{lesson:LA-C406-attentus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a task, then the Latin for clever.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: attentus, attenta, attentum}
\textbf{attentus, attenta, attentum} — \textquotedblleft{}attentive, intent; careful with money\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Discipulī attentī magistrum audiunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The attentive pupils listen to the teacher.}
\end{quote}

\emph{attentus, attenta, attentum}, the participle of \emph{attendō}, to stretch towards. \emph{Attentus ad rem}, careful with money. English \emph{attentive}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{attentus} is the participle of \emph{attendō} \textquotedblleft{}to stretch towards, to give heed\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{ad} and \emph{tendō} \textquotedblleft{}to stretch\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{attentive} and \emph{attention} come from its family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{attentus, attenta, attentum}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{attentus, attenta, attentum}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a task, then the Latin for clever, then say \emph{attentus, attenta, attentum} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[tardus, tarda, tardum]{tardus, tarda, tardum — slow; slow-witted}

\label{lesson:LA-C406-tardus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for clever, then the Latin for attentive.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tardus, tarda, tardum}
\textbf{tardus, tarda, tardum} — \textquotedblleft{}slow; slow-witted\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tardus est, sed dīligēns.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He is slow, but hard-working.}
\end{quote}

\emph{tardus, tarda, tardum}: slow of foot and slow of mind. English \emph{tardy} and \emph{retard}.

\begin{cousinweb}
The origin of \emph{tardus} is not settled; Lewis \& Short give no sure account. English \emph{tardy} comes from it through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[sēdulus, sēdula, sēdulum]{sēdulus, sēdula, sēdulum — painstaking, busy}

\label{lesson:LA-C406-sedulus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for attentive, then the Latin for slow.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sēdulus, sēdula, sēdulum}
\textbf{sēdulus, sēdula, sēdulum} — \textquotedblleft{}painstaking, busy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Sēdula ancilla domum pūrgat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The busy maid cleans the house.}
\end{quote}

\emph{sēdulus, sēdula, sēdulum}. The adverb \emph{sēdulō} is busily, on purpose. English \emph{sedulous}.

\begin{cousinweb}
The origin of \emph{sēdulus} is not settled: EtymDB links it with \emph{sedeō} \textquotedblleft{}to sit\textquotedblright{}, and Lewis \& Short call it doubtful. English \emph{sedulous} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[neglegēns, neglegentis]{neglegēns, neglegentis — careless, negligent}

\label{lesson:LA-C406-neglegens}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for slow, then the Latin for painstaking.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: neglegēns, neglegentis}
\textbf{neglegēns, neglegentis} — \textquotedblleft{}careless, negligent\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Discipulus neglegēns pēnsum nōn perfēcit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The careless pupil did not finish his task.}
\end{quote}

\emph{neglegēns, neglegentis}, the participle of \emph{neglegō}, \emph{nec} + \emph{legō}: not to pick up. English \emph{negligent} and \emph{neglect}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{neglegēns} is the present participle of \emph{neglegō} \textquotedblleft{}not to heed\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{nec} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{legō} \textquotedblleft{}to pick up, to gather\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{negligent} and \emph{neglect} come from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for slow, then the Latin for painstaking, then say \emph{neglegēns, neglegentis} again
\end{itemize}
